title: A clock that found the way

probes.question: A difference of how many degrees of longitude equals one hour of local time?
To find longitude at sea, a navigator compares local time with...
options: The time at a reference place such as Greenwich
The time of the last port visited

image.alt: The engraved gilt brass movement of John Harrison's H4 marine timekeeper on a clear display stand
image.credit: Photograph by Mike Peel (www.mikepeel.net). / Wikimedia Commons

panels.text: The Earth turns, so local time changes with longitude. A difference of 15 degrees of longitude is a one-hour difference in local time.
So a ship that knew the time at a fixed place, such as Greenwich, could compare it with local time from the Sun and work out how far east or west it was.
The catch: pendulum clocks do not work well in an ocean swell. In 1714 Britain offered prizes of £10,000 to £20,000 for a practical method.

John Harrison, a Yorkshire carpenter, built a sea clock called H4, which looked like a large pocket watch. He received payments totalling £23,065, though the £20,000 prize was never awarded in one lump sum.
